title: "Week 9 — LLMs at work"
description: "Performance, knowledge and organizational position"

## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">When an LLM helps someone do their job, what changes: their performance, their knowledge, or their position within the organization?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Weeks 7 and 8 asked whether model-generated responses reproduce observed human outcomes. Week 9 changes the unit of analysis. The model now supplies advice inside a labour process, and the empirical question concerns workers, tasks and organizations rather than synthetic respondents.

The methodological continuity remains important. We must define the target, preserve the raw model return and compare the output with external evidence. The new issue is organizational: the same underlying model can redistribute knowledge, discretion and visibility differently depending on how it is introduced.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the class, you should be able to distinguish assisted performance from retained knowledge; explain why the same technology can become part of different working arrangements; separate expertise, discretion and authority; and trace the input and output of the first student-edited Python function.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Historical and sociological anchor:** Barley (1986), “Technology as an Occasion for Structuring,” *Administrative Science Quarterly* 31(1): 78–108. Read the complete article. Barley follows the same model of CT scanner into two hospitals and shows how local occupational relations produce different divisions of labour and authority. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.2307/2392767). [@Barley1986]
- **Contemporary workplace application:** Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (2025), “Generative AI at Work,” *Quarterly Journal of Economics* 140(2): 889–942. Read the complete article. The paper studies a staggered rollout of an LLM assistant to 5,172 customer-support agents and estimates changes in measured performance while assistance is available. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044). [@BrynjolfssonLiRaymond2025]
- **Assisted performance and retained knowledge:** Wiles et al. (2026), “Generative AI and the Temporary Upskilling of Knowledge Workers,” *Nature Human Behaviour*. Read the complete article. Consultants perform unfamiliar data-science work with or without ChatGPT; a later assessment tests technical knowledge without assistance. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-026-02566-6). [@WilesEtAl2026]
:::

## Additional readings grouped by purpose

- **Algorithmic control before generative AI:** Kellogg, Valentine and Christin (2020), “Algorithms at Work.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.5465/annals.2018.0174). [@KelloggValentineChristin2020]
- **Worker experience beyond throughput:** Oder and Béland (2025), “Artificial Intelligence, Emotional Labor, and the Quest for Sociological and Political Imagination among Low-Skilled Workers.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/polsoc/puae034). [@OderBeland2025]
- **Task boundaries and overreliance:** Dell’Acqua et al. (2026), “Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2025.21838). [@DellAcquaEtAl2026Jagged]
- **Time savings and organizational coordination:** Dillon et al. (2025), “Shifting Work Patterns with Generative AI.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3386/w33795). [@DillonEtAl2025]
- **Labour behind AI systems:** Le Ludec, Cornet and Casilli (2023), “The Problem with Annotation.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/20539517231188723). [@LeLudecCornetCasilli2023]

## Sociological and methodological background

The lecture develops a cumulative argument rather than a sequence of unrelated classics. Marx and Braverman direct attention to the distribution of knowledge and control within production. Burawoy shows that workers are not passive recipients of managerial systems: consent and shop-floor practice are produced inside the organization of work. Barley demonstrates that identical technologies can become part of different occupational arrangements. Zuboff adds that computerization can perform work while creating new information about the labour process.

These distinctions matter for LLM assistance. A worker may retain formal permission to reject a draft even though the system performed much of the reasoning. A coaching interface may require more expertise from the worker without increasing their formal authority. We therefore distinguish three questions: who performs the reasoning, who chooses how to carry out the task and who has the right to make the final decision.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond report that access to the customer-support assistant increased resolutions per hour by about 15 per cent on average, with larger gains among less experienced workers. This is evidence about performance while assistance is available in one firm. Wiles and colleagues study different workers, tasks and a different design. They find better performance on assisted tasks, but no evidence of greater technical knowledge on their later unassisted measure.

The juxtaposition tells us why performance and retained knowledge must be measured separately. It does not establish that the gains in the customer-support study were unaccompanied by learning. Barley gives us another reason to remain cautious: the organizational consequences of an assistant depend on the relations, incentives and practices that form around it.

## Take-home exercise

Compare draft and coach assistance for the same customer-support case. Change one sentence in the assistance instruction, rerun both modes and explain every input, output, parameter and returned object in a narrated screen recording. Use the [recording and submission instructions](../recording-and-submission.qmd) and name the file with your name and `Week09`.

## Summary and preparation for next week

Improved performance during LLM assistance does not, by itself, show retained knowledge or a change in worker discretion and authority. Week 10 turns from workplace advice to writing, influence and relationships.
